relationship_to_protagonist: The adult Kewal: Kapoor's child role is the same man in his schooldays, so the two never share a scene and the part is a handover rather than a relationship.
relationship_to_romance: Carries all three of the film's romances; the schoolroom infatuation Kapoor plays is the first of them.
character_gist: Son of a family of lawyers who is obsessed with the theatre, submits to his father's demand that he study law, fails, leaves home to build his own theatre company, is disfigured in a fire, and narrates the whole story to his bride on their wedding night.

relationship_to_protagonist: No scenes with the child Kewal; she belongs to the adult narrative.
relationship_to_romance: The third and last of the women Kewal calls Nimmi, and the one present at the film's resolution.
character_gist: A woman made homeless by Partition whom Kewal takes into his theatre company and names Nimmi after his lost childhood love.

relationship_to_protagonist: No scenes with the child Kewal.
relationship_to_romance: The college-era Nirmala, who repeats the desertion Kapoor's segment establishes.
character_gist: The second Nirmala, met at college, who asks to be called Nimmi after hearing Kewal's story of childhood love and then abandons his play on premiere day for a marriage arranged to a man in England.

relationship_to_protagonist: Father to the boy Kapoor plays, and the pressure the child segment sets up: the family tradition of law against the child's theatre.
relationship_to_romance: No direct part in the romances; his opposition is to the vocation rather than to any of the women.
character_gist: A successful lawyer descended from lawyers who requires his son to continue the family tradition and turns him out of the house when he refuses.

relationship_to_protagonist: No scenes with the child Kewal; she frames the story he tells.
relationship_to_romance: The listener rather than a participant: the marriage that occasions the flashback.
character_gist: The bride who screams at her disfigured groom on their wedding night and to whom the entire film is narrated as a flashback.

relationship_to_protagonist: No scenes with the child Kewal.
relationship_to_romance: Outside the romances; his function is the theatre company.
character_gist: A patron of the arts who owns a shuttered theatre company and forms a creative partnership and friendship with the adult Kewal, financing the plays Kewal writes and produces.

relationship_to_protagonist: The grown Kunwar; Kapoor plays the same character as a spoiled boy, so the roles are consecutive rather than shared.
relationship_to_romance: Holds both of the film's relationships, with Kanta and with the dancing girl.
character_gist: A policeman's indulged son who grows into a casino proprietor, is blackmailed by a former accomplice, kills a dancer who betrays him, and is finally shot dead by his own father.

relationship_to_protagonist: Father to the boy Kapoor plays, and the one who intervenes when the child fires a pistol at a friend; the indulgence the child scenes show is the film's stated cause of everything after.
relationship_to_romance: No part in the romances.
character_gist: A widowed policeman who spoils his motherless son into criminality, saves him from the lock-up as a boy, and kills him at the end when the son bluffs him with an empty pistol.

relationship_to_protagonist: No scenes with Kapoor's young Kunwar; her childhood counterpart is played by Tabassum.
relationship_to_romance: The film's principal romance, and the reason for the jailbreak and abduction in the last act.
character_gist: The childhood companion, grown into a young woman, whom Kunwar meets again after fleeing a police raid and abducts from her arranged wedding.

relationship_to_protagonist: The childhood companion of the boy Kapoor plays, and his only sustained scene partner in the early stretch.
relationship_to_romance: Establishes the attachment the adult romance resumes.
character_gist: Kunwar's childhood friend, whose bond with him is the one thread the film carries from the boyhood section into the adult story.

relationship_to_protagonist: No scenes with the child; he is the adult Kunwar's nemesis.
relationship_to_romance: Threatens the marriage directly, blackmailing Kunwar as the wedding approaches.
character_gist: An old accomplice who resurfaces to blackmail Kunwar on the eve of his marriage and dies falling from a moving train during their fight.

relationship_to_protagonist: No scenes with the child.
relationship_to_romance: The competing attachment: she loves Kunwar, shelters the abducted Kanta, and turns on him out of jealousy.
character_gist: The dancing girl at Kunwar's casino, who is arrested helping him steal his mother's jewellery, gives the fugitive couple refuge, and is shot by him when she tries to alert the police.

relationship_to_protagonist: Elder brother of Kapoor's Pratap, and the brother who leaves the boy and their blind father behind to join the Indian National Army.
relationship_to_romance: Carries the film's romance, with Lily D'Souza.
character_gist: A young man so moved by Subhas Chandra Bose's call in Malaya that he buys the auctioned garland and joins the INA, leaving his blind father and small brother, and falls in love with the sister of a British spy.

relationship_to_protagonist: No scenes with Kapoor's Pratap in what the article documents.
relationship_to_romance: The romance itself: Shekhar falls for her during the song 'Gore Gore O Banke Chore'.
character_gist: The younger D'Souza sister, a dancer, with whom Shekhar falls in love, and whose sister is working for the British.

relationship_to_protagonist: No documented scenes with Pratap.
relationship_to_romance: Compromises it from the outside: the woman Suresh loves is the enemy agent inside the family Shekhar is marrying into.
character_gist: A British spy who passes as a singer, is loved by the loyalist brother Suresh, and is the elder sister of Shekhar's Lily.

relationship_to_protagonist: Eldest brother in Pratap's family, and the one who objects to Shekhar abandoning the household.
relationship_to_romance: His own attachment to Dolly sets the family against itself.
character_gist: An officer in the British Indian Army who disapproves of his brother joining the INA and is in love with the spy Dolly D'Souza.

relationship_to_protagonist: The blind father left in the boy Pratap's care when Shekhar goes to war; the pairing of the two is what gives Kapoor's child role its weight in the plot.
relationship_to_romance: No part in the romances.
character_gist: The blind father of the three brothers, left behind with his youngest son when Shekhar joins the Indian National Army.

relationship_to_protagonist: No scenes with Pratap.
relationship_to_romance: Outside the romance entirely.
character_gist: Subhas Chandra Bose, whose call to the youth of Malaya to join the Indian National Army, and whose auctioned garland, set the story in motion.

relationship_to_protagonist: The adult Raj; Kapoor plays his childhood, so the two halves of one character are divided between the brothers rather than acted together.
relationship_to_romance: Holds the film's romance with Rita, which begins in the schoolroom scenes Kapoor plays.
character_gist: Born on the streets after his mother is thrown out, drawn into theft by Jagga to feed her, grown into a skilled criminal who loves the judge's ward Rita and is finally tried for the attempted murder of the father who disowned him.

relationship_to_protagonist: Her childhood self is Kapoor's scene partner at school, before she moves away and the adult story resumes.
relationship_to_romance: The romance, and later the defence: she is both the beloved and the lawyer.
character_gist: Raj's schoolfriend, later a law student and ward of Judge Raghunath, who loves Raj knowing he is a thief and defends him at his trial.

relationship_to_protagonist: Father of the boy Kapoor plays, though he does not know it; his creed that criminals are born to criminals is the premise of the child's whole life.
relationship_to_romance: The obstacle: as Rita's guardian he is suspicious of a suitor who does not know his father.
character_gist: A wealthy district judge who holds that good people are born to good people and criminals to criminals, casts out his pregnant wife on a false suspicion, and unknowingly tries his own son.

relationship_to_protagonist: Recruits the boy Kapoor plays into theft, making him the direct author of the child's ruin.
relationship_to_romance: Obstructs it later, mocking Raj's attempts to reform and pressing him back into crime.
character_gist: The son of a criminal, wrongly convicted by Raghunath, who avenges himself by abducting the judge's wife and then by turning the judge's son into a thief.

relationship_to_protagonist: Mother of the boy Kapoor plays, and the reason the child steals; the starving mother is Jagga's lever.
relationship_to_romance: No part in the romance.
character_gist: Raghunath's wife, abducted by Jagga and cast out on suspicion of adultery, who gives birth to Raj on the streets and raises him in poverty believing he is a businessman.

relationship_to_protagonist: The boy Raj's schoolfriend and Kapoor's principal scene partner in the child section.
relationship_to_romance: Plants the attachment: the birthday picture Raj keeps into adulthood is of her.
character_gist: Raj's schoolfriend, who moves to another city after he is removed from the school rolls, and whose birthday photograph he keeps for years.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented. The film article carries no plot section and no character names, so the relation of the fifteen-year-old Kapoor's part to the leads cannot be stated.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Billed first in a vehicle built for Bharat Bhushan and Meena Kumari after the success of Baiju Bawra. The article gives no character name and no plot, so nothing further is recorded.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented; the article gives no plot and no character names.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: The female lead opposite Bharat Bhushan, uncharacterised in the article, which lists the cast without character names or a synopsis.

relationship_to_protagonist: Dilip's birth mother, who gave him up and returns years later to find the child she left has become a Muslim-hating extremist; the film's central question is whether the two can face each other.
relationship_to_romance: Not a romantic partner to Kapoor's character. Her own affair with Javed is the film's romance, and it belongs to the generation before.
character_gist: A nawab's daughter who bears Javed's child out of wedlock, gives the boy to the Rai family, later marries Javed, and comes home to a son who has become a communal fanatic.

relationship_to_protagonist: Dilip's birth father, absent for the whole of his upbringing.
relationship_to_romance: The other half of the film's one romance, with Husn Bano.
character_gist: The young man who fathers Husn Bano's child and disappears when marriage is proposed, then returns, marries her, and comes back with her to the Rai household years later.

relationship_to_protagonist: The adoptive father who gives Dilip his name and raises him as a Hindu, which is the irony the plot turns on.
relationship_to_romance: No romantic function.
character_gist: The Hindu neighbour and friend of the Nawab who helps deliver Husn Bano's son, adopts him and gives him the Rai family name.

relationship_to_protagonist: The adoptive mother who raises Dilip as her own son.
relationship_to_romance: No romantic function.
character_gist: Amrit Rai's wife, who assists at the birth of Husn Bano's child and brings him up as a Rai.

relationship_to_protagonist: Dilip's maternal grandfather, dead before the grown Dilip's story begins; he is killed protesting against British rule.
relationship_to_romance: Tries to arrange his daughter's marriage to Javed and finds the man gone.
character_gist: The Muslim nobleman whose family shares a house with the Rais, who seeks to marry his pregnant daughter to Javed and is killed during an independence protest. Played uncredited.

relationship_to_protagonist: Credited in Dilip's circle, but the article's storyline does not set out her part in it.
relationship_to_romance: The article develops no romance for Kapoor's character; romance presence is recorded as None for the film.
character_gist: Credited as Meena, with Leela Chitnis as her mother. The article's summary of the story does not describe her, so no more is recorded.

relationship_to_protagonist: The female lead opposite Kapoor's Arun, in a double part. The article has no plot section, so how the two identities relate to him is not documented.
relationship_to_romance: The romance of a film titled 'the love letter' and described as a romantic drama, but the article records nothing of its course.
character_gist: A double role, credited as Kavita Kapoor and Tara Choudhary. Seema Deo is separately credited as a Tara Choudhary, which the article does not explain.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented; the shared surname suggests a connection to Kavita Kapoor, but the article carries no plot to confirm it.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Barrister Kapoor. The article gives no plot section, so the part's function is unrecorded.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Tara Choudhary, the same name given as Sadhana's second identity. With no plot section the article leaves the duplication unexplained.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Kedar. Rajendra Nath's standing role in this period is comic support, but the article carries no plot to confirm the function here.

relationship_to_protagonist: Prem's wife by arranged marriage, and the person he is learning to be married to; her departure is the crisis of the film.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it. The film is about a marriage acquiring affection after the fact rather than a courtship.
character_gist: A young wife in an arranged marriage who cannot manage her mother-in-law's interference in the household and returns to her own family, leaving Prem to work out what a husband is.

relationship_to_protagonist: His mother, and the presence whose arrival unsettles the marriage he is still learning.
relationship_to_romance: The principal obstacle, and an internal rather than a villainous one: her interference drives Indu out.
character_gist: Prem's widowed mother, whose arrival in the young couple's home and management of it spells doom to their budding relationship.

relationship_to_protagonist: One of the several people Prem consults, and the one the article credits with the answer.
relationship_to_romance: Supplies the insight that lets Prem love his wife.
character_gist: A swami among the figures Prem turns to for guidance, who reveals to him what makes a marriage work.

relationship_to_protagonist: Among the people Prem consults about his marriage in the course of the film.
relationship_to_romance: Indirect: one of the sources of advice that shapes his idea of a husband.
character_gist: One of the figures in the Delhi world around Prem whom he approaches while trying to understand his marriage.

relationship_to_protagonist: The principal of the private college where Prem teaches, and so his employer.
relationship_to_romance: No direct part, beyond the precariousness of the job Prem is supporting a wife on.
character_gist: The principal of the private Delhi college where Prem Sagar teaches, credited with Indu Lele as Mrs. Khanna.

relationship_to_protagonist: A figure in the couple's social circle; the article's short synopsis does not detail the part.
relationship_to_romance: Not detailed by the article.
character_gist: Credited as Mrs. Saigal, with Pinchoo Kapoor as Mr. Saigal, in the Delhi milieu around the young couple.

relationship_to_protagonist: The female lead opposite Kapoor's Anand. The article has no plot section, so the course of the romance is undocumented.
relationship_to_romance: The romance of a film titled 'to whom should I give this heart' and described as a romantic comedy, though nothing of its shape is recorded.
character_gist: Credited as Sherry, the female lead. The article carries a cast list and no synopsis, so the part is not characterised.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented. Agha's double credit includes a Raja, which is also Kapoor's second identity; with no plot the article leaves the overlap unexplained.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: A double credit, Raja and Pandu, in a film whose own lead also carries a Raja identity. The article records no plot, so the doubling cannot be described.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented; Jeevan's parts of the period are usually antagonists, but the article confirms nothing.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Master. The article has no plot section and the function of the part is not recorded.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Champa. A Marathi star of the period in a Hindi supporting credit; the article gives no plot to place the part.

relationship_to_protagonist: The title character, and the senior figure in the household Kapoor's Anwar belongs to. The article carries no plot section, so the relation is not set out.
relationship_to_romance: Not Kapoor's partner; his romance is with Tanuja's Shahida, and Benazir's story runs beside it.
character_gist: The title role opposite Ashok Kumar's Nawab. With no plot section in the article the part is documented only by its billing and its name.

relationship_to_protagonist: The Nawab of the household, in a film where Kapoor's Anwar is a supporting part; the article does not state their connection.
relationship_to_romance: The senior romance of the film, with Benazir, opposite which Kapoor's is the younger pairing.
character_gist: The Nawab, first-billed with Meena Kumari. The article gives no synopsis, so the part is recorded from the cast list alone.

relationship_to_protagonist: Kapoor's romantic partner in the film, and the reason his supporting part carries a romance at all.
relationship_to_romance: The pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: a frictionless attachment running beneath the Nawab and Benazir story.
character_gist: Credited as Shahida, the young woman paired with Kapoor's Anwar. The article's brief storyline note does not follow the couple to an outcome.

relationship_to_protagonist: A member of the household; the article does not describe her dealings with Anwar.
relationship_to_romance: Structurally the obstacle to the Nawab and Benazir, being the wife, though the article does not narrate it.
character_gist: Credited as the Nawab's wife. The film article has no plot section, so the part is documented only by the credit.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Shauket. With no synopsis in the article the function of the part is unrecorded.

relationship_to_protagonist: The young actress who falls in love with Kapoor's Sanju, and the half of the triangle he ultimately fails.
relationship_to_romance: One of the film's two romances for Sanju, and the one the film treats as the loss.
character_gist: Daughter of the travelling Shakespeareana company's actor-managers, who grows up on the road performing Shakespeare in small-town India and falls in love with a rich Indian playboy already attached to a film star.

relationship_to_protagonist: Sanju's established attachment, and the woman who keeps him.
relationship_to_romance: The rival claim, and the one that prevails: she outlasts Lizzie rather than defeating her.
character_gist: A very popular Bombay film star, imperious and secure in her fame, who is romancing Sanju when Lizzie appears and does not intend to give him up.
performance_recognition: Silver Bear for Best Actress, Berlin International Film Festival, 1965.

relationship_to_protagonist: Lizzie's father and the head of the troupe Sanju is courting into; the film is loosely based on Kendal's own touring company.
relationship_to_romance: The world Lizzie would have to leave, and so a structural obstacle rather than an active opponent.
character_gist: Actor-manager of a nomadic British troupe performing Shakespeare in the towns of post-colonial India, whose real-life counterpart earned the sobriquet Shakespearewallah that gives the film its title.

relationship_to_protagonist: Lizzie's mother, and with Tony the other half of the company's management.
relationship_to_romance: Part of the family claim on Lizzie that the romance runs against.
character_gist: Tony's wife and fellow player, who oversees the touring company with him as its audiences and its country change around them.

relationship_to_protagonist: No part in Sanju's romance; he belongs to the troupe's world as a patron of the old kind.
relationship_to_romance: Outside it.
character_gist: A maharaja who receives the touring players, one of the vanishing patrons whose interest in Shakespeare sustained companies like theirs.

relationship_to_protagonist: A figure in the Indian world the troupe moves through rather than in Sanju's story.
relationship_to_romance: No direct part.
character_gist: Credited as Didi among the Indian characters surrounding the travelling company.

relationship_to_protagonist: Kapoor's wife, playing uncredited in the film that fictionalises her own family's touring company; her sister Felicity plays the woman Sanju courts.
relationship_to_romance: No part in the plot's romance, though her presence is the biographical joint between Kapoor and the Kendals.
character_gist: An uncredited appearance as Mrs Bowen by the elder Kendal daughter, by then married to Kapoor and the reason for his long association with Merchant Ivory.

relationship_to_protagonist: Father of Kapoor's Vijay, separated from him by the earthquake in infancy and absent for the whole of the son's life.
relationship_to_romance: No direct part; the family's scattering is what keeps Vijay poor and so unsuitable.
character_gist: A prosperous man who dismisses an astrologer's warning, loses his house and family to an earthquake, kills the orphanage manager who beat his eldest son, and spends years in prison.

relationship_to_protagonist: Vijay's eldest brother, unrecognised; both are in Chinnoy Seth's orbit, one as thief and one as chauffeur.
relationship_to_romance: His own romance with Meena runs parallel to Vijay's with Renu, and his discovery of Ravi's identity is what starts the reunion.
character_gist: The eldest brother, raised in an orphanage and grown into a sophisticated thief working for Chinnoy Seth, who resolves to go straight for Meena and finds that his intended rival is his own brother.

relationship_to_protagonist: The middle brother, raised by a wealthy couple, and the one who objects to Renu's involvement with Vijay without knowing the man is his brother.
relationship_to_romance: The direct opponent of Kapoor's romance for much of the film, since Renu is his foster sister and Vijay a chauffeur.
character_gist: The middle son, found on the streets and raised by a rich couple as Ravi Khanna, who becomes an advocate, is rejected as a match once his unknown parentage emerges, and leaves home after quarrelling with his foster sister over Vijay.

relationship_to_protagonist: Kapoor's romantic partner, in love with him since college and holding to it against her foster brother's objection.
relationship_to_romance: The pairing recorded in the Romances sheet, and the clearest case in the film of a couple united against the surrounding family.
character_gist: Foster sister of Ravi Khanna, in love with Vijay since their college days and unwilling to give him up over his work as a chauffeur.

relationship_to_protagonist: No romantic connection to Vijay; she is the eldest brother's attachment.
relationship_to_romance: The film's second romance, and the one whose engagement collapse exposes Ravi's parentage.
character_gist: The woman Raja loves and Ravi is to marry, whose parents break the engagement on discovering Ravi's unknown parentage and religion.

relationship_to_protagonist: Vijay's mother, the one member of the family who stays with him; the pair live in poverty after the earthquake.
relationship_to_romance: The claim on Vijay that competes with the romance, and the measure of the class distance between him and Renu.
character_gist: Kedarnath's wife, who survives the earthquake with her infant youngest son and raises him in poverty, unable to find the rest of the family.

relationship_to_protagonist: Vijay's employer, who keeps him in the chauffeur's job that makes him unmarriageable, and the criminal figure both brothers work for without knowing it.
relationship_to_romance: The circumstantial obstacle: Vijay's position in his household is precisely what Ravi objects to.
character_gist: A wealthy criminal who employs Raja as a thief and Vijay as a chauffeur, and whose house is the point where the scattered brothers converge.

relationship_to_protagonist: Part of the criminal apparatus around Chinnoy Seth that Vijay is caught up in.
relationship_to_romance: No direct part.
character_gist: One of Chinnoy Seth's men in the criminal world the brothers are entangled in.

relationship_to_protagonist: No dealings with Vijay; he governs Meena's marriage.
relationship_to_romance: Breaks the engagement between Meena and Ravi over parentage and religion, the film's plainest statement of the social test the brothers all fail.
character_gist: Meena's father, who withdraws her engagement to Ravi on discovering his unknown parentage, credited with Leela Chitnis as her mother.

relationship_to_protagonist: The heiress who rents Raja's houseboat, falls in love with him, and chooses him over her father's candidate; she also asks him to remake himself, which is the couple's one real quarrel.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of the film, and the pairing on which Kapoor's houseboat-Kashmir romantic image was built.
character_gist: Only daughter and heiress of Raj Bahadur Chunnilal, who holidays in Kashmir, befriends and then loves the houseboat owner Raja, defends the match to her father, presses Raja into a makeover that humiliates him, and finally goes to the railway station to leave with him.

relationship_to_protagonist: Rita's father, and the film's opposition: he cannot forbid the match so he engineers the rupture instead.
relationship_to_romance: The external opposition in full. He argues class incompatibility, predicts that Raja will not bear watching Rita dance with other men, and arranges the party at which exactly that happens.
character_gist: A wealthy father who wants his daughter married to Kishore, fails to reason her out of Raja, and then stages the introduction party he knows will break the couple apart; Rita overhears him admitting it.

relationship_to_protagonist: The suitor Rita's father prefers, who travels to Kashmir with her the second year and makes trouble for Raja.
relationship_to_romance: The rival claim, backed by the father and by class, and rejected by Rita.
character_gist: The wealthy match Rita's father intends for her, who accompanies her to Kashmir and is passed over for the houseboat owner. Credited under Rajesh Khanna's birth name, two years before his own stardom.

relationship_to_protagonist: Rita's maid and travelling companion, present through the Kashmir courtship.
relationship_to_romance: An attendant presence in the courtship rather than a force in it.
character_gist: Rita's maid, who accompanies her on the Kashmir holiday where she rents Raja's houseboat.

relationship_to_protagonist: Raja's younger sister, the household he supports and the measure of the simple life Rita would be marrying into.
relationship_to_romance: Part of what the class question is about: the home Rita is asked to accept.
character_gist: Raja's small sister, who lives with him on the houseboat and belongs to the village world the film weighs against Rita's.

relationship_to_protagonist: Ashok's childhood friend, brought in to impersonate a rich father so the marriage can be approved; the scheme is the plot.
relationship_to_romance: The instrument of Kapoor's romance, and the holder of the film's second one: he turns out to be the son Devraj has arranged for Malati.
character_gist: Ashok's childhood friend, disguised as the billionaire Rai Bahadur Ganga Prasad to pass as his estranged father, who is exposed as a fraud, arrested, and revealed to be the very son Devraj intended for Ramlal's elder daughter.

relationship_to_protagonist: Ashok's employer, who dismisses him for misbehaving with his daughters, and the man whose approval the whole impersonation is aimed at.
relationship_to_romance: The obstacle and the target: he intends both daughters for wealthier families, which is what forces the deception.
character_gist: A wealthy widower near Pune with two daughters and a film-struck son, determined to marry the girls into money, who dismisses his assistant manager and is then courted by a fraudulent billionaire.

relationship_to_protagonist: Ramlal's son and a fellow schemer in the household rather than an opponent of Ashok's.
relationship_to_romance: Peripheral to the romances; his own ambition is the film he wants his father to finance.
character_gist: Ramlal's elder son, who wants his father to fund a Hindi film under his own Wah Wah Productions banner and signs a village girl as his heroine; the part is among the best-remembered comic turns of Mehmood's career.

relationship_to_protagonist: Kapoor's romantic partner, the younger daughter, whom he first offends and then falls in love with.
relationship_to_romance: The pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: antagonism in the household turning into attachment.
character_gist: Ramlal's younger daughter, a matriculate, with whom the dismissed assistant manager camped in the front yard eventually falls in love, and who is married to him in the general reconciliation.

relationship_to_protagonist: The elder daughter, one of the two Ashok is accused of misbehaving with, but not a romantic interest of his.
relationship_to_romance: Holds the parallel romance, being matched by her father with Devraj's missing son.
character_gist: Ramlal's elder daughter, a science graduate, whose marriage her father arranges with the son of his old schoolfellow Devraj, the son being Shyam.

relationship_to_protagonist: No romantic connection to Kapoor's Ashok; she belongs to Atma's film-production strand.
relationship_to_romance: Outside the two marriages the plot resolves.
character_gist: A village belle and daughter of Ramlal's property manager, signed by Atma as the female lead of his proposed production.

relationship_to_protagonist: Ashok's real father, and the truth the impersonation exists to hide.
relationship_to_romance: The disclosure that collapses the scheme and, briefly, the marriage.
character_gist: A poor schoolteacher, Ashok's actual father, whose existence Devraj uncovers and reveals to Ramlal, exposing Rai Bahadur as a fraud.

relationship_to_protagonist: The woman Kapoor's Anwar courts among three suitors and wins, and the person kept in the dark about his father's trade.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it; the film is her choice among three candidates and then the collapse of the ground under it.
character_gist: The daughter of a noble Delhi household with three suitors, who falls in love with Anwar after a few outings, and whose parents learn on the wedding day that his family's nobility was bought with a lottery win.

character: Ajju Hajam / Nawab Ajmutullah Khan Farooqui
relationship_to_protagonist: Anwar's father, and the secret the marriage rests on: a barber who assumed the title of Nawab after winning a lottery.
relationship_to_romance: The concealed obstacle. His past, not any rival, is what threatens the wedding.
character_gist: A barber by trade who took the title of Nawab after a lottery win and so got his son onto the approved list of suitors, credited opposite Manorama as his Begum.

relationship_to_protagonist: Nishat's father, who vets the suitors and initially rejects Anwar before restoring him to the list.
relationship_to_romance: The gatekeeper: the approval he grants on a false premise is withdrawn on the wedding day.
character_gist: A Delhi nobleman who judges his daughter's suitors by family standing, admits Anwar on the belief that his background is noble, and learns the truth as the wedding begins.

relationship_to_protagonist: One of the two rejected suitors, and genuinely of the class Anwar only appears to belong to.
relationship_to_romance: A rival claim with the father's approval behind it.
character_gist: Son of Nawab Hamid Khan and the suitor Nishat's father approves of, displaced by Anwar and resentful of it.

relationship_to_protagonist: The third suitor, a relative of Nishat's mother, and the comic side of the competition.
relationship_to_romance: A rival claim, family-backed and never serious.
character_gist: A distant relative of Nishat's mother, approved as a suitor on that account, and left aggrieved with Shaukat when she chooses Anwar.

relationship_to_protagonist: Nishat's mother, part of the parental judgement on the suitors.
relationship_to_romance: Shares the approval and the wedding-day discovery.
character_gist: Nishat's mother, whose own relative is among the approved suitors, and who learns with her husband what Anwar's family actually is.

relationship_to_protagonist: The neighbour who first takes him for a stalker, then marries him, then spends the rest of the film fearing he will kill her.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: a marriage held under suspicion of murder.
character_gist: A wealthy neighbour who finds Gopal annoying and believes he is following her, falls for him anyway, defies her brother to marry him, survives an attempt on her life on honeymoon, and then learns her husband was tried for killing his first wife.

relationship_to_protagonist: Sapna's brother, who wants her married elsewhere and threatens to kill her when she refuses.
relationship_to_romance: Direct opposition, and one of the two candidates for the film's real conspirator.
character_gist: Sapna's brother, who intends her for Prem, threatens her life when she chooses Gopal instead, and remains a suspect in the attempts on her afterwards.

relationship_to_protagonist: The suitor Sapna's brother prefers, and the other man who threatens her when she chooses Gopal.
relationship_to_romance: The rival claim, and part of the web of lies that makes the marriage a danger.
character_gist: The match Pran intends for Sapna, who threatens to kill her when she refuses him and is implicated in the campaign of suspicion around her husband.

relationship_to_protagonist: The police presence around a man already acquitted of one wife's murder.
relationship_to_romance: Indirect: the investigation is what finally clears the marriage.
character_gist: The inspector on the case around Deepak Verma, whose first trial ended in acquittal and whose second wife is now being targeted.

relationship_to_protagonist: Comic relief in the neighbourhood around the couple, credited with Shammi as his wife.
relationship_to_romance: No part in the suspense plot.
character_gist: A neighbour in the Bombay setting, paired with Shammi's Itabai, providing the comic register against the murder plot.

relationship_to_protagonist: The Englishwoman whose romance with Kapoor's Singaporean guide is the film's subject, and who leaves at the end.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, from her side: the affair is an episode in her release rather than a destination.
character_gist: A repressed young Englishwoman travelling as companion to her wealthy spinster aunt, who is left alone in Singapore by the aunt's sudden death and pursues her freedom, and an arm's-length romance with a local guide.

relationship_to_protagonist: Second-billed in the Singapore world Polly is loosed into; the article's two-sentence synopsis does not set out his dealings with Amaz.
relationship_to_romance: Not described by the article.
character_gist: Credited as Robert Hook, with Brenda de Banzie as Mrs. Innes-Hook. The article's synopsis is two sentences long and does not place the part.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented. The synopsis names the wealthy aunt whose death frees Polly but does not map her to a credit.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Mrs. Innes-Hook. The article does not identify which credit belongs to the aunt whose death begins the story, so the part is recorded without that inference.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented by the article's synopsis.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Rick Preston. The article carries a full cast list but almost no plot, and separately lists the cast of another production of the same source, which is not this film's.

relationship_to_protagonist: Loves and marries the decent twin, Kamal, having first mistaken him for the one who torments her; she then cannot tell which man has come home from the war.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: a marriage attacked by an impostor who is the husband's own double.
character_gist: A widower's daughter who moves to a new city, is teased by Rakesh, complains by mistake about his lookalike Kamal, marries Kamal, and after the war subjects the man claiming to be her husband to tests he fails for reasons of his own.

relationship_to_protagonist: The film's comic lead alongside Kapoor's double role.
relationship_to_romance: Comic counterpoint to the courtship rather than a participant.
character_gist: Ghasitaram Aashiq, the comic figure of the college and estate world the twins move through, paired in the credits with Ameeta's Laali.

relationship_to_protagonist: Outside the central triangle, which is filled on both sides by Kapoor himself.
relationship_to_romance: Belongs to the film's secondary comic pairing.
character_gist: Credited as Laali, daughter of the character played by Yunus Parvez, in the film's lighter second strand.

relationship_to_protagonist: The college authority in the early section, where Archana's misdirected complaint sets the confusion going.
relationship_to_romance: The mistaken complaint that starts the romance passes through him.
character_gist: The professor at the college where Archana meets the twins, and part of the machinery of the opening mix-up.

relationship_to_protagonist: Archana's widowed father, friend of Rakesh's father, whose consent she seeks for the marriage to Kamal.
relationship_to_romance: Grants the consent the marriage needs, and owns the estate where the couple's honeymoon and the later impostor episode take place.
character_gist: Archana's widowed father, who moves with her to the new city and gives his consent to her marriage with Kamal.

relationship_to_protagonist: The village woman Kumar loves, deceives with his own name, and then tells the truth to; the deception is that his full name really is Amar Kumar.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: a courtship turned by a childhood marriage nobody told her about.
character_gist: A village girl who shelters a stranded traveller and falls in love with him, learns she was married in childhood to a man named Amar, accepts her fate, leaves with Kumar on the evidence of his full name, and walks out when he admits the other Amar is alive and married.

relationship_to_protagonist: Kumar's friend and namesake, the man Kumar married off to Lata, and unknowingly Rekha's childhood husband; the shared name is the plot.
relationship_to_romance: The impediment in person. His existing marriage is what Kumar is protecting when he lies to Rekha.
character_gist: A hockey player who loves Lata and is married to her through Kumar's good offices, and who turns out to be the Amar to whom Rekha was married as a child.

relationship_to_protagonist: The woman Kumar promises her father he will look after, having no in-laws to do it; that promise is the obligation that makes the truth unspeakable.
relationship_to_romance: The marriage that must be protected, and so the reason Rekha cannot be given her actual husband.
character_gist: Amar's wife, married to him at Kumar's initiative, whose settled household is what the disclosure of Rekha's childhood marriage would destroy.

relationship_to_protagonist: The one who tells Kumar of the childhood marriage, hands him the wedding photograph, and asks him to find the missing husband.
relationship_to_romance: Springs the obstacle, and unknowingly supplies the means of the deception.
character_gist: Rekha's mother, who reveals that her daughter was married as a child to a man named Amar, gives Kumar the wedding photograph, and asks his help in tracing him.

relationship_to_protagonist: Second-billed after Kapoor and Parekh, in the comic register around the two Amars.
relationship_to_romance: No part in the impediment plot.
character_gist: Credited as Bansi, with Tun Tun as his mother-in-law, carrying the comic line of a film otherwise built on a marital deadlock.

relationship_to_protagonist: Meets him three times under three names, changes her mind about the false Jhatpat Singh, and rekindles the romance when he turns up as the estate manager.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: an identity comedy resolved into a family reunion and a wedding.
character_gist: The only child of the widowed Mohan, adopted by the heirless Sardar Ranjit Kumar, who meets a young man in Ooty as Pyarelal, again as a false Jhatpat Singh, and finally as her grandfather's estate manager, and marries him.

relationship_to_protagonist: Sunder's mother, who eloped against her father's will and loses her reason after the fire; her recovery closes the film.
relationship_to_romance: Structurally decisive rather than active: the restoration of her identity is what makes the marriage possible.
character_gist: Ranjit's daughter, who eloped with the peasant Gopal, is reconciled to her father too late, loses her husband in the fire and her son to the night, and regains her sanity at the reunion.

relationship_to_protagonist: Sunder's father, burned to death in the opening movement, and the reason the boy grows up adopted and nameless.
relationship_to_romance: The precedent: a marriage across class that the family destroyed, which the younger romance repeats on better terms.
character_gist: The poor peasant with whom Jamuna elopes, found burned to death in the flames that consume their house on the night her father comes to be reconciled.

relationship_to_protagonist: The grandfather who does not know him, who appoints him estate manager and then intends Seema for an impostor.
relationship_to_romance: The obstacle in the last act: he wants Seema married to Shankar's son, whom he believes to be the lost grandson.
character_gist: A landowner without an heir who disowns his eloping daughter, adopts his employee's child Seema, and is deceived into accepting his step-brother's son as the grandson he lost.

relationship_to_protagonist: The step-brother who plants his own son in Sunder's place to take the property, making him the rival for both the inheritance and Seema.
relationship_to_romance: Direct opposition: the marriage he engineers for his son is to the woman Sunder loves.
character_gist: Ranjit's estranged step-brother, who passes his son off as Jamuna and Gopal's lost child in order to take the estate, and nearly secures Seema for him.

relationship_to_protagonist: The man whose name Kapoor's character borrows, whose arrival in Ooty makes Seema change her mind.
relationship_to_romance: The mechanism of the middle act: his appearance collapses the borrowed identity.
character_gist: The actual Jhatpat Singh, to whom Seema was supposedly engaged in childhood, credited alongside Rajendra Nath's fake Jhatpat Singh in a plot where the name passes through several hands.

relationship_to_protagonist: Attached to the real Jhatpat Singh rather than to Sunder.
relationship_to_romance: No part in it.
character_gist: A small acting appearance by the film's own composer, one of only two such parts in his career, the other being Bhoot Bungla.

relationship_to_protagonist: The woman Pritam falls for, who has already settled on another man, and who comes round to him by way of her uncle.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: a suit won over an incumbent rather than against a villain.
character_gist: A young woman who has already chosen Ajit as her partner when Pritam falls for her, and whose affections shift once Pritam has won over the uncle who speaks for the family.

relationship_to_protagonist: The figure Pritam must win, and the route to Deepali; the comic encounters with him are the film's method.
relationship_to_romance: The decisive ally rather than an obstacle: he converts family opinion and with it Deepali.
character_gist: Deepali's uncle, whose good opinion Pritam secures through a series of comic encounters and who then helps him win her.

relationship_to_protagonist: The man Deepali has already chosen when Pritam appears, and so the incumbent Pritam displaces.
relationship_to_romance: The rival claim, and the one the film's comedy works around rather than through violence.
character_gist: The partner Deepali has settled on before Pritam's arrival, displaced in the course of Pritam's campaign for the family's favour.

relationship_to_protagonist: Third-billed comic support around Pritam's pursuit.
relationship_to_romance: Comic accompaniment to the courtship.
character_gist: Credited as Ram Bharose Agnihotri in the comic apparatus of a film built on a suitor's campaign for a family's approval.

relationship_to_protagonist: A senior family presence in the household the courtship is conducted in.
relationship_to_romance: Part of the family opinion Pritam must carry.
character_gist: Credited as Rama among the family around Deepali, in the household whose approval decides the match.

relationship_to_protagonist: Outside the courtship proper; Helen's parts of this period are usually a dance number and a complication.
relationship_to_romance: Peripheral to the central suit.
character_gist: Credited as Sherry. The article's short synopsis covers only Pritam's campaign for Deepali and does not place the part.

relationship_to_protagonist: The princess Raju is made to impersonate a prince in front of, who comes to love him, and from whom the truth is withheld.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: an attachment built on an imposture the film leaves unresolved.
character_gist: A princess courted by a man she takes for Prince Pratap Singh, who after initial hesitation returns his feeling, and whose response to learning he is an orphan and a pauper the article's synopsis poses as a question.

relationship_to_protagonist: Raju's employer, and the man he is compelled to impersonate; the whole deception is his instruction.
relationship_to_romance: The author of the romance and its flaw, since the courtship is conducted in his name.
character_gist: The prince who employs Raju and forces him to stand in for him before Princess Poonam, setting up an imposture that outgrows its purpose.

relationship_to_protagonist: The family authority over Poonam, and so over the credibility of the borrowed royal identity.
relationship_to_romance: The standing that the imposture exists to satisfy.
character_gist: Poonam's uncle, the family authority whose expectations about rank the impersonation is designed to meet.

relationship_to_protagonist: Poonam's secretary, placed close enough to the courtship to be part of its management.
relationship_to_romance: An attendant presence in the courtship.
character_gist: Poonam's secretary, credited among the household through which the false prince conducts his courtship.

relationship_to_protagonist: Comic support in the world around the imposture, credited with Kumari Naaz as Hameshbahar.
relationship_to_romance: No part in the central courtship.
character_gist: Credited as the father of Kumari Naaz's Hameshbahar, in the comic register of an impersonation plot.

relationship_to_protagonist: His long-standing friend and now his fiancee, who trusts him deeply and is nonetheless worked on until she accuses him.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: an engagement with no internal conflict at all, damaged entirely from outside.
character_gist: An heiress living with her widowed mother, engaged with her mother's blessing to a poor young man she has known for years, who is slowly made afraid that he wants her property, confronts him at the lawyer's office, and must win him back after the accusation drives him away.

relationship_to_protagonist: The cousin who wanted him for herself and, refused, set out to destroy his engagement; she is the film's entire opposition.
relationship_to_romance: The manipulator. Every doubt in the relationship is placed there by her, which is why the pairing scores high on external opposition and near zero on friction between the couple.
character_gist: Neeta's cousin, who warns her repeatedly that Sudhir is after her money, stages the visit to the lawyer that seems to prove it, and finally confesses that she loved him herself before taking poison and dying in Neeta's arms.

relationship_to_protagonist: Approves of him and consents to the marriage, which is unusual for a poor suitor in this period of Kapoor's work.
relationship_to_romance: Support rather than obstacle: her consent removes the standard family objection and leaves the field to Naina.
character_gist: Neeta's widowed mother, who gives her consent to her daughter's marriage with a poor young man.

relationship_to_protagonist: Neeta's other cousin and Sudhir's friend, who vouches for him and is the intended beneficiary of the property transfer that looked like theft.
relationship_to_romance: Clears it: he confirms to Neeta how Naina poisoned her mind.
character_gist: A cousin with a passion for stage and theatre who recommends Sudhir warmly, and to whom Sudhir was quietly transferring Neeta's property so as not to touch a penny of her money.

relationship_to_protagonist: A household presence around the courtship.
relationship_to_romance: No part in the manipulation plot.
character_gist: Credited as Neeta's maidservant, in the comic register of a household drama.

relationship_to_protagonist: The stage dancer he marries, who gives up her career for him and takes it back when he neglects her; the marriage's strain is hers as much as his.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: a marriage that has to find again what it lost, rather than a courtship.
character_gist: An established stage dancer and singer, orphaned early, who meets an assistant scientist by chance, marries him with his mother's approval, gives up performing, resumes it when he retreats into the laboratory, separates from him, and reunites for his mother's sake.

relationship_to_protagonist: His mother, living apart from him, whose approval makes the marriage and whose visit ends the separation.
relationship_to_romance: The opposite of the interfering mother-in-law the period specialises in: she sanctions the match at the start and is the reason the couple reconcile at the end.
character_gist: Shekhar's mother, who lives separately, approves of the dancer her son wants to marry, and whose arrival in her old age brings the separated couple back under one roof.

relationship_to_protagonist: Belongs to the scientific world that absorbs Shekhar's time; the article's synopsis does not detail the part.
relationship_to_romance: Indirect: the laboratory is what Anjana is competing with.
character_gist: Credited as Dr. Niranjan Das, in the research world where Shekhar spends the time his wife wants.

relationship_to_protagonist: The only family the orphaned Anjana has, on her side of the marriage.
relationship_to_romance: A family presence rather than a force; the synopsis gives him no part in the strain.
character_gist: Credited as Anjana's uncle, the guardian figure for a woman the film describes as orphaned at an early age.

relationship_to_protagonist: No part in the marriage plot.
relationship_to_romance: Appears in the song 'Milte Hi Rahenge Hum', in the performing career that is the marriage's rival.
character_gist: A dancer in the song 'Milte Hi Rahenge Hum', credited for that appearance alone.

relationship_to_protagonist: The woman he escorts across the country and falls in love with while she is in love with a poet she has never met; his feeling is not returned during the journey.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet as unrequited: the film is built on the gap between the man beside her and the man in the poems.
character_gist: A young woman returning from the United States who survives an engine flameout, cannot separate the poet Ujjwala from his poetry, and runs away from the psychiatric treatment her father arranges in order to reach Phulwari and meet him.

relationship_to_protagonist: The pursuing authority for the whole journey: the reward he announces is what turns bystanders into obstacles for Sunil and Sapna.
relationship_to_romance: The engine of the external opposition, though his target is his daughter's obsession rather than Sunil.
character_gist: Sapna's wealthy father, who consults a psychiatrist about her distraction, agrees to have her committed for an extended period, and announces an informant's reward once she runs. The article separately credits Randhir as Rana Randhir Singh Chauhan, the name its own synopsis gives the father.

relationship_to_protagonist: No direct dealings with Sunil; his diagnosis is what puts Sapna on the road.
relationship_to_romance: Sets the journey going, and with it the courtship.
character_gist: The psychiatrist consulted about Sapna, who pronounces that she needs treatment and must be sent to his clinic for an extended period.

relationship_to_protagonist: The danger on the road, in a film whose obstacles are mostly greed and accident.
relationship_to_romance: One of the dangerous interludes the couple pass through together.
character_gist: A dacoit encountered on the journey, providing the film's genuine threat among its comic ones.

relationship_to_protagonist: One of the coachload of travellers thrown together with Sunil and Sapna for the journey.
relationship_to_romance: The audience to the courtship, and part of the greed the reward provokes.
character_gist: One of the bus passengers, a company that also includes David, Manmohan Krishna, Leela Mishra, Master Bhagwan and Sunder, who make up the travelling ensemble of the road journey.

relationship_to_protagonist: The woman the Nairobi musician meets at a function and falls in love with.
relationship_to_romance: The pairing recorded in the Romances sheet. The article's plot is three sentences long, so the course of the triangle is not documented.
character_gist: The woman Raj Kumar Rai meets at a function and loves, credited with Sulochana Chatterjee as her mother. The article gives no more of her story.

relationship_to_protagonist: The woman who loves him without being loved in return, which is the whole of the triangle the article records.
relationship_to_romance: The competing claim, and the reason the relationship is classified as a love triangle.
character_gist: Credited as Rani Mehta, daughter of Raj Mehra's Mr. Mehta, and named by the article's short synopsis as the woman in love with Raj Kumar.

relationship_to_protagonist: Third-billed, in the family register Nirupa Roy occupies throughout this period, though the article's three-sentence plot does not state the relation.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Durga, third in the billing. The article carries almost no plot, so the part's function is not recorded.

relationship_to_protagonist: Shares the surname of Kapoor's Raj Kumar Rai, which suggests the father, though the article does not confirm it.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Mr. Rai. The shared surname with the protagonist is the only evidence of the relation, and the article's synopsis does not address it.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented by the article, which gives three sentences of plot.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Pran Mehra, in the Mehta and Mehra circle around the romance. Madan Puri's standing function in this period is the antagonist, but the article does not confirm it here.

relationship_to_protagonist: Credited with Manorama and Pinchoo Kapoor as his parents, forming a comic family unit alongside the main story.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Tom Genda, with a mother and father of his own in the cast list, in the comic register of a film set among Indians in Nairobi.

relationship_to_protagonist: The female lead opposite a triple role. The article, titled Jahan Pyar Miley, gives a cast list with no character names and no plot, so nothing of the relation is documented.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented. Romance presence is left blank for the film for the same reason.
character_gist: Billed second, opposite Kapoor's three credited identities. The article supplies no character names and no synopsis, so the part cannot be described.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented; the article maps no credit to a character.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Third-billed. With no character names and no plot in the article, the function of the part is recorded as unknown rather than inferred from the actress's usual casting.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Fourth-billed in a cast list without character names. Jeevan's parts of the period are usually antagonists, but the article gives no basis for stating it here.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited among the principals in a cast list that gives no character names, in a film whose article has no plot section.

relationship_to_protagonist: The British writer who has an affair with Kapoor's married film star; she is also Kapoor's own wife, playing opposite him for Merchant Ivory.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: a triangle in which the star is the object rather than the pursuer.
character_gist: A British author researching the Bombay film industry, who falls in love and into an affair with the married star Vikram while his friend Hari is in love with her.

relationship_to_protagonist: Vikram's friend, and the man whose love for Lucia complicates the affair.
relationship_to_romance: The third point of the triangle, and the one with the weakest claim.
character_gist: Vikram's friend, a writer in love with Lucia Lane, whose feeling goes unreturned while she pursues the film star.

relationship_to_protagonist: Vikram's wife, and the fact that makes the affair an adultery rather than a courtship.
relationship_to_romance: The standing obstacle, present as a marriage rather than as an opponent.
character_gist: The wife of the film star Vikram, whose existence is what the article names as the complication in his affair with Lucia.

relationship_to_protagonist: Belongs to the film-industry world Vikram works in and Lucia is researching.
relationship_to_romance: No direct part in the triangle.
character_gist: Credited as Bose, among the figures of the Bombay film industry that the British author has come to study.

relationship_to_protagonist: A figure of the industry around Vikram, credited under the name Florence Ezekiel.
relationship_to_romance: No direct part in the triangle.
character_gist: Credited as Anjana Devi, one of the film-world portraits the picture assembles around its star.

relationship_to_protagonist: No scenes of consequence with Vikram; the appearance is uncredited and precedes his own stardom.
relationship_to_romance: No part in it.
character_gist: An uncredited mourner, four years before Deewaar made him Kapoor's most frequent co-star. The same appearance is his third screen credit.

relationship_to_protagonist: Both women in the film: the shy sister he marries and the vivacious one he actually met and fell in love with, which is why the film generates two pairing rows from one performer.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, on both sides. The playful Kashmir courtship and the marriage poisoned by mistaken identity are the same actress in a double role.
character_gist: Twin sisters: Kanchan, shy and drawn to animals and nature, whose marriage prospects keep collapsing when suitors meet her sister, and Kamini, witty and forward, who sneaks into an army base for supplies, is caught by Captain Ajit, and is smitten with him before leaving without giving her name.

relationship_to_protagonist: Ajit's foster father, called Baba, who proposes the marriage that sets the mistaken identity going.
relationship_to_romance: The unwitting author of the confusion: he is the one person Kanchan speaks to candidly and the one who matches her with Ajit.
character_gist: The town priest, confidant of the shy Kanchan and foster father of Captain Ajit, who brings up the subject of marriage with his returning son and says he knows just the girl.

relationship_to_protagonist: The film's villain against Ajit's household, in what is also among Ranjeet's early parts.
relationship_to_romance: Threatens the marriage from outside, alongside the confusion the sisters create inside it.
character_gist: Credited as Kundan, the antagonist of a film whose central trouble is nonetheless a case of mistaken identity rather than villainy.

relationship_to_protagonist: Ajit's commanding officer, in the army setting where he first meets Kamini.
relationship_to_romance: Presides over the base where the courtship begins.
character_gist: The colonel of the army camp in Kashmir whose supplies Kamini comes to steal and whose captain assists her.

relationship_to_protagonist: Part of the threat around Ajit's marriage rather than a rival for either sister.
relationship_to_romance: External danger to the couple.
character_gist: Credited as Tiger, among the film's antagonists.

relationship_to_protagonist: The woman he loves and then deliberately repels for his benefactor's sake; she holds to him while he pushes her away.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: a couple kept apart by the hero's own debt of gratitude.
character_gist: A young woman who mistakes Shyam for a thief on a train, grows close to him, and turns out to be the double of the dead Kamla whom Shyam's benefactor loved; she refuses to marry Amar Singh for her family's security and waits for Shyam's proposal while he drinks to drive her off.

relationship_to_protagonist: Shyam's benefactor, who educated a servant's son and treats him as a brother, and who becomes the reason Shyam gives up Renu.
relationship_to_romance: The obstacle and finally the resolution: his own attachment to Renu's dead sister makes him the family's preferred match, and his discovery of the couple's feelings is what frees them.
character_gist: A prince who raised and educated his servant's son as a brother, stayed a bachelor for love of the dead Kamla, takes in her family, and is shaken to find Renu her exact likeness.

relationship_to_protagonist: Shyam's father and a servant in the palace, which is the class fact the whole obstacle rests on.
relationship_to_romance: Presses for the match that suits the household rather than his son: he too hopes Amar Singh will finally marry Renu.
character_gist: Ramu kaka, a servant in Amar Singh's palace and Shyam's father, who sees in Renu the likeness of Kamla and hopes his master will at last marry.

relationship_to_protagonist: The petty thief whose stolen purse gets Shyam accused, and so the cause of the couple's first misunderstanding.
relationship_to_romance: Starts the romance by accident, then holds the film's second one.
character_gist: A petty thief who plants Renu's purse in Shyam's coat, turns out to be Renu's lost cousin, is reconciled to the family, and falls in love with Chandan Singh's sister Rajkumari.

relationship_to_protagonist: Sister of the Chandan Singh whose insult at Shyam's low birth creates the film's rivalry.
relationship_to_romance: Holds the secondary romance, with Kuldeep, across the same class line.
character_gist: Chandan Singh's sister, whose hand Amar Singh asks for Shyam, giving offence because Shyam is a servant's son, and who falls in love with Kuldeep instead.

relationship_to_protagonist: Part of the household taken in by Amar Singh, and among those urging Renu towards the secure marriage.
relationship_to_romance: Family pressure on Renu's side, pushing her towards the benefactor and away from Shyam.
character_gist: Renu's aunt, brought with the rest of the bereaved family into Amar Singh's house, and among the relatives who want Renu married to him for their security.

relationship_to_protagonist: The woman he loves and marries across a blood feud, and the mother of the child he later stakes out as bait.
relationship_to_romance: The pairing recorded in the Romances sheet, and secondary to the tiger plot: the marriage is achieved early and then subordinated to the hunt.
character_gist: The daughter of the man who killed Shekhar's father, who falls in love with him, is barred from marrying him until her father is dead, marries him at a ceremony the tiger interrupts, and bears his son Raju.

relationship_to_protagonist: Meena's father and his own father's killer, which is the single fact blocking the marriage.
relationship_to_romance: The external opposition entire, and removed by being killed rather than reconciled.
character_gist: Meena's father, who had killed Shekhar's father years earlier, making the marriage impossible until Mohan kills him and the past is forgiven.

relationship_to_protagonist: His widowed mother, with whom he lives while managing the estate.
relationship_to_romance: The household the marriage enters, and a widow made so by Meena's father.
character_gist: Shekhar's widowed mother in Jamuna Nagar, widowed by the killing that later stands between her son and the woman he loves.

relationship_to_protagonist: The one who kills Gokuldas and so clears the way for Shekhar's marriage.
relationship_to_romance: Removes the obstacle by violence, which is what makes the union possible.
character_gist: Credited as Mohan, and named by the article as the man whose killing of Gokuldas allows the marriage to proceed.

relationship_to_protagonist: His infant son, and the object of the film's last act: Shekhar decides to use the child as live bait for the man-eater.
relationship_to_romance: The issue of the marriage, and the thing the hunt finally puts at stake.
character_gist: Shekhar and Meena's small son, born about a year after the wedding, whom his father resolves to stake out as bait when no adult volunteers.

relationship_to_protagonist: Attached to the estate household through the hunt.
relationship_to_romance: No part in the marriage plot.
character_gist: Credited as Bahadur, carrying the comic line of a film otherwise built on a man-eating tiger and a blood feud.

relationship_to_protagonist: The courtesan through whom Siddhartha passes into sensual pleasure and material life; she is a stage of his search rather than a destination.
relationship_to_romance: The pairing recorded in the Romances sheet, and explicitly subordinate: the film is a spiritual quest in which the love affair is one of several conditions tried and set down.
character_gist: A celebrated courtesan who takes Siddhartha as a lover and draws him into the world of pleasure and wealth that he later turns from in self-revulsion.

relationship_to_protagonist: His companion from the beginning of the search, and the friend who takes the other road, following a teacher where Siddhartha will not.
relationship_to_romance: Outside it.
character_gist: Siddhartha's friend and fellow seeker, whose willingness to follow a master measures Siddhartha's insistence that the secret of life cannot be passed from one person to another.

relationship_to_protagonist: The ferryman beside whom Siddhartha arrives at the harmony he has been seeking, and a teacher who teaches by not teaching.
relationship_to_romance: Outside it.
character_gist: The ferryman at the river, in whose company Siddhartha comes to the oneness with himself that neither asceticism nor pleasure nor wealth had given him.

relationship_to_protagonist: The merchant who employs him, and so the agent of the material-wealth stage of the search.
relationship_to_romance: Belongs to the same worldly phase as Kamala.
character_gist: The merchant in whose service Siddhartha acquires the material wealth that becomes the third thing he must renounce.

relationship_to_protagonist: Siddhartha's son in the film, and Kapoor's own son in life, appearing as a child.
relationship_to_romance: The issue of the relationship with Kamala.
character_gist: Siddhartha's son, played as a child by Kapoor's elder son Kunal, who would later act in Paap Aur Punya and Junoon.

relationship_to_protagonist: The Brahmin father whose house and expectations Siddhartha leaves at the start of the search.
relationship_to_romance: Outside it.
character_gist: Siddhartha's father, credited with Shanti Hiranand as his mother, the rich family the young man leaves in order to look for a meaningful way of life.

relationship_to_protagonist: His second wife, according to the cast list. The article has no plot section, so what the marriage consists of is undocumented.
relationship_to_romance: The living half of a marital structure the cast list sets out and the article never narrates; no Romances row was created for the film on that account.
character_gist: Credited as Ravi's second wife. The film article carries a cast list and no synopsis, so the part is documented only by that relation.

relationship_to_protagonist: His first wife, given in the cast list as already dead when the story begins; she is the title of the film.
relationship_to_romance: The absent presence the title names, though the article gives no account of her part in the story.
character_gist: Credited as Ravi's first wife and marked deceased, the character whose name the film carries. With no plot section the article leaves her function unstated.

relationship_to_protagonist: His father, a raja, per the cast list.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Ravi's father, a raja, which is the whole of what the article establishes about the household.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented; the article gives her no character name.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited without a character name, alongside David Abraham Cheulkar, in a cast list the article does not support with any synopsis.

relationship_to_protagonist: The woman he teases, wins, becomes intimate with and proposes to, and who is then made to believe he wanted money for the marriage; she bears his son believing the child stillborn.
relationship_to_romance: The whole of it, and the pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: a relationship broken and kept broken by her father's forgery rather than by anything between them.
character_gist: A young doctor in Bombay living with her widower father, who meets a skater in Simla, is saved from hypothermia by him and becomes intimate, accepts his proposal, is shown a letter her father has rewritten to make him a fortune-hunter, becomes engaged elsewhere, and gives birth to a son she is told did not live.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented. The film article carries a cast list with no plot section, which is also why romance presence is left blank for the film and no Romances row was created.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Amba, the principal female part opposite Kapoor's Arjun. The article gives no synopsis, so nothing further is recorded.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Allah Rakhi. The article has no plot section and the function of the part is unrecorded.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as Kirpal, among the senior supporting parts of a film whose article carries no synopsis.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not documented, beyond the police function the credit names.
relationship_to_romance: Not documented.
character_gist: Credited as a police inspector, with Ram Mohan as Abdul Police, indicating a crime setting the article otherwise does not describe.

relationship_to_protagonist: The woman he woos against her initial refusal, and who joins him and Ram in the plan against Raghuveer.
relationship_to_romance: The pairing recorded in the Romances sheet, and secondary to the revenge plot: the courtship is complete before the film's real business begins.
character_gist: The woman Dilip spends his carefree days pursuing, who rebuffs him at first and then loves him, and who takes part in the scheme to reach the circus owner who murdered his family.

relationship_to_protagonist: His lifelong friend, and the man whose father turns out to be the murderer Dilip is hunting; the friendship is what the film puts at stake.
relationship_to_romance: Outside the romance; his marriage to Asha is the settled counterpart to Dilip's courtship.
character_gist: Dilip's close friend since boyhood, married to Asha, who discovers that the criminal his friend has sworn to destroy is the father who abandoned him and his mother twenty years earlier.

relationship_to_protagonist: The escaped convict who murdered Dilip's father, mother and siblings, and the object of the revenge that drives the second half.
relationship_to_romance: No direct part, beyond the danger the courtship is conducted under.
character_gist: A notorious criminal sentenced by Dilip's real father, who escaped prison, murdered the judge's whole family, and now owns a circus under the name Diwan; he is also Ram's father.

relationship_to_protagonist: The wealthy man Dilip believes to be his father, whose deathbed disclosure converts the film from a romance into a revenge story.
relationship_to_romance: Was arranging Dilip's marriage to Poonamchand's daughter, which the courtship of Leena was running against.
character_gist: Dilip's supposed father, who raises him in wealth and tries to marry him to his friend Poonamchand's daughter, and who tells him on his deathbed that he is not his son.

relationship_to_protagonist: Mother of his closest friend, and abandoned twenty years earlier by the man Dilip means to kill.
relationship_to_romance: No part in it.
character_gist: Ram's mother, left by Raghuveer twenty years before the story, and the other person whose life the revenge would cut through.

relationship_to_protagonist: The loyal servant who, pressed, tells Dilip who his real parents were and how they died.
relationship_to_romance: No part in it.
character_gist: The household's loyal servant, who under prodding gives Dilip the history of the judge, the convict and the murders.

relationship_to_protagonist: Dilip's actual father, dead before the story, whose sentence on Raghuveer caused the massacre of his family.
relationship_to_romance: No part in it.
character_gist: The judge who sentenced Raghuveer to a long term and was murdered with his wife and children when the man escaped; Dilip is the surviving son.

relationship_to_protagonist: The rich girl he loves, who is matched elsewhere by her father and reconnects with him after his escape.
relationship_to_romance: The pairing recorded in the Romances sheet: a couple against her father and a politician, with no conflict of their own.
character_gist: The wealthy daughter of Jagdish, in love with a poor engineer, promised instead to the son of a politician, and reunited with Vijay after he breaks out of the jail he was framed into.

relationship_to_protagonist: Rekha's father, who rejects him for poverty and then helps frame him for a crime he did not commit.
relationship_to_romance: The opposition, and the one character who reverses: he repents at the end and accepts Vijay as his son-in-law.
character_gist: Rekha's father, who disapproves of a suitor without money, arranges her marriage to an evil politician's son, joins in framing Vijay, and finally feels remorse and accepts him.

relationship_to_protagonist: The politician whose son is Rekha's intended and who engineers the false charge that jails him.
relationship_to_romance: The active opposition, working through Rekha's father.
character_gist: An evil politician whose son is to marry Rekha, who frames Vijay for a crime, terrorises the village of Shantinagar with bandits, and is arrested at the end.

relationship_to_protagonist: One of the three prisoners who become his friends and escape with him, and who return to jail with him voluntarily at the end.
relationship_to_romance: Outside the romance; the prison friendship is the film's other relationship.
character_gist: One of the three convicts Vijay befriends inside, who breaks out with him, helps save Shantinagar from the politician's bandits, and goes back to prison with the others.

relationship_to_protagonist: Another of the escaped prisoners, in the comic register of the group.
relationship_to_romance: No part in it.
character_gist: One of Vijay's fellow prisoners, credited with Tarun Ghosh's Kalua in the band that escapes and then defends the village.

relationship_to_protagonist: Not detailed by the article's summary, which follows the frame-up and the village rescue.
relationship_to_romance: No part in the central courtship.
character_gist: Credited as Chandramukhi, in the world of the jail break and the terrorised village that the film's second half occupies.

relationship_to_protagonist: The poor woman the heir loves and intends to marry, and whom the changed Ganga abandons for the rich match.
relationship_to_romance: The pairing recorded in the Romances sheet as forbidden love: the obstacle is dynastic, and the article's synopsis ends on her question rather than a resolution.
character_gist: A young woman from a poor family who loves the prince Ganga Singh and is to marry him, set aside when he abruptly turns dissolute and agrees to wed the wealthy Mala, and left by the article's own summary asking what she will do.

relationship_to_protagonist: The usurper who ordered the killing of his brother's son, and the father of the prince Kapoor plays; he is both parent and villain.
relationship_to_romance: The opposition: he will have nothing to do with a poor bride and intends Mala for his son.
character_gist: The brother who overthrows the fair-minded Raja Gajraj Singh, orders his infant nephew killed, arranges the fatal accident of Gajraj and his wife, and rules unchallenged while grooming his own son for the throne.
